strengths: Significance: Inference-time mitigation without retraining addresses a useful deployment problem. Separating verbatim and template memorization exposes substantial differences that aggregate evaluation could conceal.

Empirical merits: Table 1 shows meaningful improvements. CA-in-GUARD reduces SSCD to 0.079 on SD v1.4 verbatim memorization, versus 0.113 for the strongest listed baseline, and to 0.193 on SD v2.0 template memorization, versus 0.260. The attention-only variant also improves substantially over Ren et al. on template memorization.

Originality: Prompt-dependent spike detection provides a useful extension beyond fixed EOT/padding interventions. The block, head, timestep, and alternative-target ablations help characterize the proposed design.

Presentation and ethics: The framework is generally understandable, and the paper explicitly distinguishes independently optimized metrics from joint trade-offs. Appendix A.1 appropriately acknowledges that inference-time mitigation does not erase information or protect against white-box extraction.
weaknesses: Soundness and reproducibility: The central detector is described inconsistently. Sections 5.2–5.3 compute spatial maxima of attention probabilities from the unmodified conditional branch, whereas Appendix A.2 computes Z-scores on the attenuated branch's pre-softmax logits. These differ in both statistic and source activations, particularly after earlier interventions. The aggregation across heads/blocks and treatment of BOT/padding are also insufficiently specified. This prevents a reliable reconstruction of the actual method.

Mechanistic support: Multiplying selected logits by a factor below one does not necessarily attenuate their attention: negative logits increase toward zero, and the operation depends on the arbitrary additive offset of logits. The manuscript does not establish the conditions under which its intervention suppresses the intended tokens. Figures 1 and 6 provide illustrative attention patterns, but no dataset-level validation that detected spikes specifically identify memorization triggers rather than ordinary semantic attention.

Evaluation and reproducibility: Hyperparameters are optimized separately for each model/memorization category, with no reported held-out validation/test split. Thus the results establish performance after benchmark-specific tuning, not reliable deployment on unseen prompts of unknown memorization type. Appendix A.2 supplies ranges but omits grid resolution, selected configurations, baseline search budgets, guidance scale, and sampler details; the promised code URL is blank.

Attribution and originality: The incremental benefit of repulsion is not isolated from changing guidance strength. Equation 5 can be rewritten as unconditional prediction plus (s−r) times the attenuated conditional direction, plus r times the difference between attenuated and original predictions. A matched effective-guidance comparison is needed to distinguish the proposed mechanism from simply weakening conditioning. The novelty of the general guidance arithmetic is also less clearly established than that of its attention-based instantiation.

Quality preservation is not convincingly established. FID uses only 288–572 generated images per setting against 10,000 unrelated LAION images, making it sensitive to small-sample estimation and prompt-distribution mismatch. There is no qualitative generation comparison or human evaluation. Appendix A.3 tests benign prompts only for CA attenuation, not full CA-in-GUARD; the latter changes effective guidance even when no spikes are detected. Consequently, this experiment cannot substantiate benign-input quality preservation for the headline method.

Claims exceed the evidence. On SD v1.4 template memorization, Han et al. achieves lower SSCD than CA-in-GUARD (0.479 versus 0.517), and the appendix acknowledges a better SSCD–CLIP trade-off. On verbatim prompts, CA-in-GUARD's best-SSCD configuration reduces CLIP from 0.346 to 0.266. These results support useful mitigation with trade-offs, rather than consistent dominance or no quality loss. Both tested models are closely related Stable Diffusion U-Nets, limiting architectural generality.

Protection remains insufficiently characterized: Mean SSCD against one associated training image does not measure the residual extraction rate, worst-case prompts, or copying of other training examples. Four generations per prompt and no adaptive black-box evaluation provide limited evidence for robust protection. The honest white-box limitation is appropriate, but the broader safety claims require stronger evidence.

strengths: Significance: Inference-time mitigation without retraining addresses a useful practical problem. Separating verbatim and template memorization exposes differences that aggregate evaluations could obscure, and filtering for initially high SSCD focuses the evaluation on difficult cases.

Empirical merits: Table 1 shows substantial improvements in selected settings. For SD v2.0 template memorization, CA-in-GUARD reaches SSCD 0.193 versus 0.260 for the strongest listed baseline at its best-SSCD configuration. For SD v1.4 verbatim memorization, it reaches 0.079 versus 0.113. These results support further investigation.

Originality: Prompt-adaptive attention-spike selection is a plausible extension beyond fixed EOT/padding interventions. The block, head, timestep, and alternative-positive-target ablations provide useful evidence about implementation choices.

Presentation and ethics: The main framework is understandable, and Figure 2 explicitly warns that independently optimized metrics do not represent one jointly achievable configuration. Appendix A.1 appropriately acknowledges that inference-time mitigation does not erase information from weights or protect against unrestricted white-box access; this is an honest scope limitation.
weaknesses: Soundness—quality preservation is insufficiently established. FID uses only 288, 572, or 384 generated images against 10,000 randomly sampled LAION images. With such small generation sets and an unmatched reference distribution, FID is a weak basis for claims about realism and diversity. No qualitative generation examples or human evaluation corroborate these claims. Semantic alignment also decreases substantially in some configurations: on SD v1.4 verbatim memorization, best-SSCD GUARD reduces CLIP from 0.346 to 0.266. The selection protocol permits this because its threshold comes from a different prompt population. The evidence supports a mitigation–utility trade-off, not the abstract's unqualified claim of avoiding quality harm.

Soundness—the complete method is not evaluated on non-memorized prompts. Appendix A.3 tests only CA attenuation. When no spikes are detected, the positive and negative predictions coincide, so Equation 5 becomes ordinary CFG with scale s−r rather than s. Thus, the benign-prompt results cannot establish that CA-in-GUARD preserves normal generation. A full-method evaluation on ordinary prompts and a reduced-CFG baseline are needed to separate benefits of the proposed repulsion from changes in effective guidance strength.

Reproducibility—the algorithm has materially inconsistent descriptions. Section 5.3 computes spikes from the unmodified conditional stream, whereas Appendix A.2 computes statistics from the spike-attenuated stream within each attention layer. These streams differ after upstream interventions, so the descriptions need not implement the same method. Aggregation across heads and blocks and treatment of BOT/padding in spike statistics are also unclear. Moreover, multiplying a negative logit by a factor below one increases it, so the stated operation does not universally suppress selected attention weights.

Reproducibility and statistical validity: No held-out tuning/evaluation split is described for the small, filtered prompt sets. Table 2 supplies search intervals but not grid points, selected configurations, or comparable baseline search budgets; the guidance scale and sampler are not specified. The code-availability sentence ends without a link. Confidence intervals are described as being across four generations, leaving uncertainty across prompts unclear. These omissions limit both replication and confidence in best-configuration comparisons.

Mechanistic evidence and originality: Attention spikes are not shown to identify memorization-specific triggers rather than ordinary semantic salience. Figure 1 compares memorization types using different model versions, confounding the proposed mechanistic distinction, and Appendix A.5 bases its localization illustration on three prompts. Dataset-level analyses and matched random-token or top-attention controls are needed. The guidance equation is a straightforward combination of conditional predictions; its distinctive contribution therefore depends heavily on validating the detector and its incremental benefit.

Presentation and significance—the strongest comparative claims exceed the results. For SD v1.4 template memorization, Han et al. achieves better SSCD than GUARD (0.479 versus 0.517), with slightly better CLIP and FID at those configurations. Appendix A.8 acknowledges a corresponding Pareto exception, yet the main text repeatedly claims consistent dominance. The experiments cover two related U-Net Stable Diffusion versions, providing limited support for broad architectural robustness. Table 5 also shows roughly 41–45% runtime overhead for GUARD, qualifying the claim of efficiency close to a single forward pass.

Protection claims require narrower interpretation. Mean similarity to one associated training image does not measure the frequency of residual near-copies or exclude reproduction of other training examples. Four generations per prompt and no adaptive black-box extraction evaluation establish average mitigation on this benchmark, not reliable protection against extraction. The privacy motivation is reasonable, but stronger safety language needs tail-risk measurements and an explicit evaluated threat model. Together with the methodological and reproducibility issues above, this prevents acceptance despite the promising empirical gains.

strengths: Significance: Inference-time mitigation without retraining addresses a useful practical problem. Separating verbatim and template memorization exposes meaningful differences that aggregate evaluation could obscure.

Originality: Prompt-adaptive attention-spike detection combined with attractive–repulsive guidance is a plausible methodological contribution. The observation that EOT-focused interventions transfer poorly to template memorization provides useful motivation.

Empirical merits: Table 1 reports substantial improvements, including SSCD reductions from 0.356 for Ren et al. to 0.193 for CA-in-GUARD on SD v2.0 template memorization. Comparisons with four baselines, Pareto plots, and block/head/timestep ablations provide several complementary evaluations.

Presentation and ethics: The high-level framework is understandable, and the captions explicitly distinguish independently optimized metrics from joint trade-offs. Appendix A.1 appropriately acknowledges that inference-time mitigation does not erase information or protect against white-box access.
weaknesses: Soundness and reproducibility: The detector has materially inconsistent definitions. Sections 5.2–5.3 compute spikes from attention weights in the original conditional stream, whereas Appendix A.2 describes computing statistics on the attenuated stream's logit tensor. These differ in both the source stream and the measured quantity. Aggregation across heads/blocks and treatment of special tokens also need precise specification.

The attenuation rationale is not generally valid as stated: multiplying a negative logit by a factor below one increases that logit and can increase its attention weight. High relative attention does not guarantee a positive logit. The paper should establish when its operation suppresses selected tokens and quantify whether detected spikes identify memorization-specific information rather than ordinary semantic salience.

Evaluation and reproducibility: Hyperparameters are tuned separately for each architecture–memorization setting, but no held-out selection protocol is described. Reporting the best observed configurations therefore does not establish performance on unseen prompts with a fixed configuration. Appendix A.2 provides ranges without complete grids or selected settings, omits baseline search details, and leaves the promised code URL blank.

The central quality-preservation claim is insufficiently supported. Appendix A.3 tests only CA attenuation on non-memorized prompts, not CA-in-GUARD. This distinction matters: when no spikes are detected, Equation 5 reduces to ordinary CFG with scale s−r, so full GUARD can still change benign generations. On memorized prompts, Table 1 also shows appreciable alignment loss; SD v1.4 verbatim CLIP falls from 0.346 without mitigation to 0.266.

Quality and privacy measurements have important gaps. FID uses only 288–572 generated images against 10,000 general LAION images, making it sensitive to finite-sample effects and distribution mismatch. There are no generated-image comparisons or human assessments to corroborate quality. Mean SSCD against the associated training image does not establish low residual copying rates or exclude copying other images; failure-rate and tail analyses are needed.

Presentation overstates consistency and scope. On SD v1.4 template memorization, Han et al. achieves better SSCD than GUARD, 0.479 versus 0.517, with slightly better CLIP and FID in Table 1. Two closely related U-Net Stable Diffusion versions also provide limited evidence for broad architectural robustness. Table 5 shows roughly 41–45% runtime overhead for GUARD, which warrants clearer qualification of the efficiency claims.

Overall, the contribution is promising, but unresolved implementation ambiguity and missing evidence for the full method's generalization and utility preservation prevent acceptance. These concerns concern support for central claims, rather than the honestly acknowledged limitation of leaving model weights unchanged.

strengths: Significance: Inference-time memorization mitigation is a useful problem, and adapting attention interventions to individual prompts is practically motivated. Separating verbatim and template memorization exposes weaknesses that aggregate evaluation can obscure.

Originality: The combination of token-level attention outlier detection, selective attenuation, and contrastive guidance offers a concrete methodological contribution. The observation that EOT-focused interventions transfer poorly to template memorization provides useful additional understanding.

Empirical merits: Table 1 shows substantial improvements over relevant baselines, particularly for SD v2.0 template memorization: CA-in-GUARD achieves SSCD 0.193 versus 0.260 for Wen et al. The appendix adds full-spectrum evaluation, DINO retrieval, sampler and guidance ablations, runtime measurements, and exploratory SD v3.0 results.

Presentation and ethics: The manuscript clearly distinguishes the framework from its attention-based instantiation and explicitly distinguishes independently optimized metrics from joint trade-offs. Appendix A.1 appropriately acknowledges that inference-time mitigation does not erase information or protect against white-box access; this is a legitimate scope limitation.
weaknesses: Soundness—central implementation ambiguity: Sections 5.2–5.3 define spike detection using attention distributions from the unmodified negative conditional stream, whereas Appendix A.2 computes statistics on the spike-attenuated positive stream's logits. These differ both in the source trajectory and potentially in using logits versus normalized attention. Head/block aggregation and treatment of special tokens are also insufficiently specified. Consequently, the actual algorithm underlying the reported results is unclear.

Soundness—guidance confounding: Equation (5) can be rewritten as unconditional prediction plus (s−r) times the original conditional direction plus s times the difference between modified and original predictions. Thus increasing repulsion also reduces effective ordinary guidance. The reported CFG ablation does not isolate this effect with matched effective-guidance controls. Moreover, when no spikes are detected, the method still changes CFG from s to s−r. Appendix A.3 tests only CA attenuation on non-memorized prompts, leaving the full method's claimed benign-input quality preservation unvalidated.

Evaluation and reproducibility: Hyperparameters are selected separately for each architecture and memorization category, with no reported held-out selection/evaluation split or transfer of a fixed configuration. Table 2 provides ranges but not grid resolutions or selected configurations, and comparable baseline search budgets are unspecified. The code availability statement ends with an empty link. SD v3.0's adaptation to joint attention is not described sufficiently to reproduce. These omissions materially limit confidence in generalization and fair comparison.

Quality evidence is insufficient for the strongest claims. FID uses only 288, 572, or 384 generated images in the main settings against 10,000 unrelated LAION reference images, making it vulnerable to small-sample bias and content-distribution mismatch. Table 1's verbatim CLIP decreases from 0.346 without mitigation to 0.266 with GUARD; the chosen reference permits this despite the claim of avoiding quality degradation. Larger, appropriately matched quality evaluations are needed.

Presentation overstates empirical dominance. For SD v1.4 template memorization, Table 1 reports worse SSCD for GUARD than Han et al. (0.517 versus 0.479), with similar CLIP and FID. For SD v2.0, GUARD ties standalone attenuation on SSCD, while Wen et al. has better FID at the SSCD-selected configurations. Appendix A.7.2 acknowledges an exception that conflicts with repeated claims of consistent superiority across settings.

Mechanistic and protection claims exceed the evidence. Illustrative attention plots and downstream improvements do not establish that detected spikes specifically identify memorization-critical tokens; matched random-token or attention-based selection controls would strengthen this interpretation. Mean similarity reductions over four generations also do not establish protection against repeated sampling or prompt variations. Residual copying rates and tail-risk evaluation are needed to support deployment-facing protection claims.

strengths: Significance: Inference-time mitigation of training-image reproduction is a useful problem. Prompt-specific attention intervention offers a practical contribution without retraining or access to the original training pipeline.

Empirical merits: Table 1 shows substantial improvements in several settings. CA-in-GUARD achieves SSCD 0.079 for SD v1.4 verbatim memorization, compared with 0.113 for the strongest listed baseline, and 0.193 for SD v2.0 template memorization, compared with 0.260. Table 7 also reports favorable results across the full 500-example benchmark.

Originality: The strongest contribution is the adaptive token-level intervention and the investigation of differences between verbatim and template memorization. The block, head, timestep, and alternative-target ablations provide useful empirical understanding beyond proposing another guidance formula.

Presentation and evaluation breadth: The main framework is accessible, and Figure 3 explicitly acknowledges that independently optimized metrics need not be achieved simultaneously. The appendix includes Pareto curves, DINO measurements, runtime measurements, and exploratory SD v3.0 results.

Ethics and limitations: The privacy motivation is appropriate, and Section A.1 correctly acknowledges that inference-time mitigation leaves memorized information in the weights and cannot protect against unrestricted white-box access.
weaknesses: Soundness and reproducibility: The detector is described inconsistently. Section 5.3 computes attention statistics from the original conditional stream, whereas A.2 computes them from the spike-attenuated stream itself. Those streams diverge after earlier interventions and can identify different tokens. It is also unclear how attention statistics are aggregated across heads and modules. Multiplying selected logits by a factor below one does not universally reduce their attention probability: negative logits increase toward zero. The implementation needs an unambiguous specification and evidence that the intended suppression occurs.

Evaluation reliability: Hyperparameters are optimized separately for each architecture, memorization category, and target metric, but no held-out tuning/evaluation split is described. Table 2 gives ranges without grid resolution or selected configurations, and comparable baseline search budgets are not documented. Consequently, the results establish benchmark-tuned performance more clearly than transferable performance. The code-availability statement in A.2 ends without a link, making these omissions materially harder to resolve.

Unsupported superiority claims: The repeated claim of dominance across settings exceeds the reported evidence. For SD v1.4 template memorization, Table 1 gives Han et al. better SSCD, CLIP, and FID than CA-in-GUARD: 0.479 versus 0.517, 0.188 versus 0.186, and 210.839 versus 210.983. Figure 13 also shows this competitive limitation. Additionally, Table 5 reports Wen et al.'s SD v2.0 'best FID' as 197.186 although its best-SSCD configuration already achieves a better FID of 188.914. Such inconsistencies undermine confidence in the configuration-selection results.

Quality preservation is insufficiently established: Table 1 reduces verbatim CLIP from 0.346 without mitigation to 0.266 with CA-in-GUARD. The acceptance threshold is based on a different prompt distribution, so satisfying it does not demonstrate preservation relative to the original outputs. FID uses only 288–572 generated images in the main subsets against 10,000 broadly sampled LAION images, making it sensitive to finite-sample bias and distribution mismatch. Table 3 evaluates ordinary prompts only for CA attenuation, not the full GUARD method.

The repulsion mechanism is not adequately isolated: Equation 5 can be rewritten as unconditional prediction plus (s-r) times the attenuated conditional direction, plus r times the difference between attenuated and original predictions. Thus, changing r also changes effective guidance strength. A matched-guidance control is needed to distinguish the proposed mechanism from ordinary guidance rescaling; the reported scale ablation does not clearly provide this comparison.

Statistical and protection claims need tighter scope: Mean similarity over four generations does not establish a low probability of reproducing a training image. Residual-copy rates, per-prompt tails, and larger sampling budgets would better support the protection claims. The confidence-interval construction does not clearly explain its treatment of prompt-level versus seed-level variability. DINO provides useful corroboration, but the retrieval corpus and implementation are insufficiently specified.

Generalization to SD v3.0 remains preliminary: A.8 evaluates only 39 prompts selected using a different similarity threshold and omits the architectural details needed to reproduce the attention intervention in the transformer backbone. These results are promising, but do not yet substantiate broad architectural robustness.

strengths: Significance: Inference-time memorization mitigation is a useful problem, and prompt-adaptive attention intervention offers a practical approach without retraining or access to the original training pipeline.

Originality: The strongest contribution is the adaptive selection of attention spikes, motivated by differences between verbatim and template memorization. This provides useful understanding beyond fixed EOT-token suppression.

Empirical evidence: Table 1 shows substantial improvements, including SD v1.4 verbatim SSCD of 0.079 versus 0.113 for the strongest baseline, and SD v2.0 template SSCD of 0.193 versus 0.260. Full-spectrum results, DINO metrics, and sampler/block/head/timestep ablations strengthen the evidence.

Presentation: The framework and its concrete instantiation are clearly separated, and the paper explicitly distinguishes individually optimized metrics from joint trade-offs. The appendix provides extensive numerical results and runtime measurements.

Limitations and ethics: Appendix A.1 appropriately acknowledges that inference-time intervention does not erase information from model weights or protect against white-box extraction. The privacy-oriented motivation is reasonable, with no evident material ethical concern.
weaknesses: Soundness—quality preservation is insufficiently established. Table 1 reduces SD v1.4 verbatim CLIP from 0.346 to 0.266; the selection protocol permits this by using a different reference score. FID compares only 288–572 generated images against 10,000 unrelated LAION reference images, making it sensitive to small-sample estimation and distribution mismatch. These results support a mitigation–quality trade-off more clearly than the abstract's claim of avoiding quality loss.

Soundness—the contribution of repulsion is confounded with reduced effective guidance. Equation 5 equals CFG on the attenuated prediction with scale s−r, plus r times the difference between attenuated and original predictions. When those predictions coincide, GUARD simply reduces CFG to s−r. A matched-effective-guidance comparison against CA attenuation is needed; varying the nominal CFG scale in Appendix A.6 does not isolate this effect.

Reproducibility: Section 5.3 detects spikes from the original conditional stream, whereas Appendix A.2 computes them from the spike-attenuated stream. These differ after earlier interventions. Attention aggregation across heads/blocks and adaptation to SD v3.0 are also underspecified. The code availability sentence has no link, and Table 2 supplies search intervals without exact grids or selected configurations.

Evaluation reliability: Hyperparameters are selected separately for each architecture/memorization setting on the reported benchmark, with no stated held-out validation protocol or complete baseline search budgets. The confidence-interval description does not clearly distinguish variation across prompts from variation across four generations. This limits confidence in generalization and close comparisons.

Mechanism and deployment: Attention spikes are treated as memorization-critical without population-level detector validation or a matched random-token intervention. Table 2 even uses Z-score thresholds of 0.01–0.05 for verbatim CA attenuation, far from conventional outlier thresholds. Appendix A.3 evaluates non-memorized prompts only for CA attenuation, leaving the full GUARD method's collateral effects untested.

Claim calibration: Dominance across settings is overstated. For SD v1.4 template memorization, Han et al. achieves better SSCD than GUARD (0.479 versus 0.517), with comparable or slightly better CLIP/FID. The SD v3.0 extension uses only 39 prompts. Together with the unresolved methodological issues, these limitations warrant revision before acceptance despite the promising empirical contribution.
